topics.title: Radio Fans Battle Trivia
topics.summary: Two radio fans, Mr. Bill and Radio Fan, compete in a trivia contest with Howard Stern, answering questions about NBC history, celebrity encounters (including Jessica Hahn), and pop culture references like the ‘Kill, Kill, Kill the Hippies’ poem. The competition highlights their knowledge of past shows and personal interactions.

topics.title: Radio Trivia Show Chaos
topics.summary: A radio show hosts a trivia game with listeners resulting in arguments and confusion over answers. The conversation drifts from military service to Howard Stern’s past appearances on Rolling Stone magazine culminating in an attempt to determine the name of a bar associated with a former NBC employee.”} 29 words

topics.title: Jethro’s Military Ambitions and Wife Troubles
topics.summary: During the broadcast, Jethro expresses a desire to join the military, leading to him being enrolled in a Cub Scout troop instead. The conversation then veers into bizarre tangents involving urine tests, drug use within the military, concerns about his wife's potential affairs, and financial exploitation – including a planned marriage with a telephone salesman.

topics.title: Telephone Salesman Reveals Odd Story
topics.summary: A phone salesman, Ernie, recounts a bizarre encounter involving insurance sales and a strange conversation with Spanky McFarlane. He details confusing listeners with Mexican heritage references, an army drug test where only he failed, childhood accidents, and a scarred brother before devolving into nonsensical questions.

topics.title: Limo Driver’s Central Park Incident
topics.summary: A limo driver recounts a bizarre incident where he accidentally discarded his underpants into a Central Park tree while transporting Keith Hernandez. He then attempted to clean the situation with Windex, leading to confusion and questioning whether anyone would believe his story.

topics.title: Callers Critique Ferraro and Mock Dinkins
topics.summary: During a radio broadcast, callers express negative opinions about Geraldine Ferraro’s campaign for vice president, citing her awkwardness on camera and associating her with ‘bad New York politics.’ They make crude observations regarding her appearance and detail rumors of bribery involving her husband, while one caller describes disturbing details about a neighbor's skin condition. A comedic imitation of Dickie Goodman follows, filled with offensive jokes and impersonations.
